items.title: The Search Committee
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Two big, long-in-the-making additions to this site today. Whee!

The first is the addition of House committees and their transcripts. Committees can be really interesting. Even though this current Parliament certainly doesn't mark their heyday, they're still the most productive part of the House. There's way less theatre and name-calling than in debates—and, unlike in the House chamber, nobody's ever speaking to a vast empty room. And since they revolve around external witnesses, you can hear some surprising perspectives that go beyond the familiar party talking points.

Adding committees about doubled the amount of data we have, so I figured the search engine needed a bit of a facelift to deal with it. I ended up doing full reconstructive surgery. The new search does quite a bit more than its predecessor. It's not easy designing a search interface to be powerful and information-dense without also being complicated and overwhelming, and so feedback and suggestions are very welcome…

items.title: Nocturnal Catboat
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Some 60 years ago this week.

Operation Market Time. 29 November 1966.

Official Caption: A Cat Lo-based U.S. Navy large personnel landing craft (LCPL) cruises in Vung Tau Harbor during an Operation Market Time patrol. The LCPL is armed with a 50-caliber air-cooled machine gun.

Note the gun is fitted with twin spotlights, useful in night patrols, cued to targets by the craft’s on-board radar.

Photographer’s Mate Second Class Whitmarsh took this photo on 29 November 1966. USN 1120032

While the Navy had acquired 2,193 original LCP(L)s for amphibious use in WWII, built by Higgins Industries and licensed small yards (Chris-Craft, Matthews, Owens Yacht, and Richardson Boat), the 305 assorted post-war LCPL variants bought from the late 1950s through the early 1970s (primarily built by Marinette Marine) were used more for command, control, patrol, and UDT/SEAL support.

items.title: Does Nature abhor a vacuum? And the avalanche of easy papers
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
“Nature abhors a vacuum”, Aristotle wrote (although not quite in those words, mostly because English hadn’t been invented yet, but also because he was rarely that succinct). But does it? For millennia this has been a difficult hypothesis to test, but two recent developments have changed that. The more recent is the rise of electronic journal indexing, and of the software tools needed to scrape data from those indices. The less recent, but even more important, was the founding in 1869 of the journal Nature.

So does Nature abhor a vacuum? I searched for all papers in Nature published between 1960 and 2026 that included the word “vacuum” in title, keywords, or abstract. There were 415 of them, so it’s clear that if Nature abhors a vacuum it doesn’t do so absolutely.

But Nature could still abhor a vacuum in relative terms (or if you prefer, it could still moderately dislike a vacuum). So I did the same search for Science, the closest thing there is to a comparator journal for Nature. Of…

Christmas isn’t even as exciting anymore, aside from maybe the decorations. Different corporate companies keep publishing their holiday sale ads everywhere. I think I’ve seen more ads through email and commercials this year than in previous years. Is it just me who’s noticing that?

The state of my divided family relationships reminds me of how lonely the holidays have become for me. I know that’s the core of my problem here. It’s complicated, but I’m trying to heal from the trauma. I’ve been prioritizing self-care with coloring…

I was watching the show Pantheon recently, and something got me curious.

Minor spoilers ahead

At some point in the show, the protagonist sets up her own private wireless network that isn't connected to the internet. She even installs what appear to be signal transmitters on lamp posts and other places to extend the network's coverage.

I know it's possible to have a local network without an internet connection, but I've always associated that with relatively confined environments, such as an office, a classroom, or a home and my knowledge of networking and computer systems isn't particularly advanced, so I'm curious about how feasible something like this would be in real life.

Could someone realistically build an independent wireless network covering a neighbourhood or even an entire town? What kind of hardware and infrastructure would be needed? Would something like a wireless mesh network accomplish this? What would the practical limitations be in terms of range, bandwidth…

items.title: Verbose Mode
items.label: Showcase
items.excerpt:
I just started a new blog where I can post about the process of developing software and tech in general. My first proper article is Runtime Quality Requires Humans which is about the limitations of trying to use AI coding with complex systems. I built a new site because I was tired of dealing with ads and paywalls on sites like Medium.

This was also an experiment in using the Astro web framework to make a complex static site, which worked out really well. I wrote all of the article myself but around half of the website tech was written by Claude Code, which I talk about on the About page. If anyone has feedback or a question, I'd love to hear it here!

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.

Cook cleverly, plan badly, or just roll with it — the dragon doesn't care how you win, only that you feed the beast on time. And yes, you can pet the…

items.title: Juice Galaxy (formerly Juice World) [$5.00] [Role Playing] [Windows] [macOS] [Linux]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
Juice is everything. There is nothing in the Fog. There is no greater honor than to serve the Juice Queen, and the sky is definitely not made of plywood.

Juice Galaxy is a happy place to fly around and smack things and drink juice. And explore things. And just, flip around doing stuff. Use any of a multitude of weapons to clobber and devour the local wildlife. Gather juice to increase your power and take on more powerful enemies.The game is still in active development. There's still a ton of work to do. I want to polish the physics and add a ton more abilities, places, music, items, monsters, and story.Enjoy, and please feel free to leave feedback or suggestions.
